source.title: Geometric Routing Enables Causal Expert Control in Mixture of Experts

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or cutoff; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures how many experts have clear, coherent specializations in a small MoE model and reports a much lower share than the claim's roughly 90% figure, alongside a large polysemantic share. This challenges the claim's extension to MoE models, though its unit and measurement differ.
record.gate_note: The study's manual classification of decoded expert outputs bears on the proposed prevalence of interpretable units in MoE models. Cited findings are not recorded as results. The causal interventions and routing analyses do not measure the shares in V2 or test the specific attribution-graph claim in V5.
record.test_reason: The study classifies all 8,192 rank-1 experts, each effectively a single-neuron unit, in a small MoE language model by how coherent their decoded output is. That is a different method aimed at the share of single-job units in an MoE model, so it bears on V2. It is not a T5 argument against the version: the authors present the result as support for monosemanticity.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim that rank-1 MoE experts are 'architecturally monosemantic' and that steering, suppression and surgery validate the labels causally. They say cosine routing makes expert function readable from the centroid matrix, while linear routers allow similar steering. They limit these claims to 76–84M WikiText-103 models with rank-1 experts.
record.recipe_differences: The study decodes expert output vectors through the unembedding matrix and manually classifies their top-10 vocabulary words. It does not explain Qwen3 neuron poles or test explanations on held-out activations.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering, suppression and surgery of dictionary-labelled experts shift the probability of the target category (e.g. temporal steering median +321%; geographic surgery −45.8%). These are causal checks on labels for selected experts, not shares of interpretable units.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Output-decoded labels of MoE experts are causally valid for selected experts.

record.problems: The share estimate is based on manual inspection of decoded top-10 words, not held-out activation tests. The model is small, trained on WikiText-103, and uses rank-1 experts; its expert categories are not directly comparable to neuron poles. No uncertainty estimate is reported for these shares.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported results concern routing, steering, suppression, expert surgery, and compositional interventions; they do not measure the shares named in V2 or test the specific claims in V1 and V3–V7. Cited results are also omitted.

untested.parts: Dense models, standard full-rank MoE experts, models above 84M parameters up to trillions, and neuron-pole explanations built from activating examples. Only output-weight decoding of one 76–84M rank-1 MoE trained on WikiText-103 is tested.

missing.what: In HDBSCAN clustering of decoded expert centroids, 73.5% of experts remain unclustered. Only 20 extra clusters are found, and 7 of 16 novel clusters were tested by steering. This is relevant to how many experts have a coherent, identifiable job.

record.verdict_notes: There is a tension in the paper: it calls the experts 'monosemantic by construction' yet classifies 65% as moderately polysemantic. The tool here is weak (output-side logit lens, top-10 words, manual judgment, no held-out activation test, no inter-rater reliability). V4 would attribute a low share partly to tools, which is why the label is limits_scope rather than challenges. The paper also offers no dense baseline, so it cannot test V4's architecture claim.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit and its neuron-pole proportions.
Dense models, larger MoE models, and models up to trillions of parameters; the study tests only its own 76–84M-parameter MoE model.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose detection, and recursive generalization.
The InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates and the causal roles of architecture, regularization, and tools.
Attribution graphs, explaining model behavior with them, and comparison with a trained replacement model or reconstruction error.
Whether explanations from activating examples predict where neurons fire on held-out activations.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: ST-M O E
rows.operation_detail: Manually classified experts by the coherence of their top-10 decoded vocabulary words after projecting output vectors through the unembedding matrix.
rows.measure: Share classified as clear monosemantic specialists
rows.note: This is an expert-level classification from decoded vocabulary, not an audit of neuron poles or an explanation tested on held-out activations.
rows.check: The value is correct (about 15% clear specialists). The criterion is stricter than 'one main job': all top-10 decoded output words must fall in one category, judged from the output side only. The share is therefore likely a lower bound on single-job units, not a direct counterpart of the 90% figure.

rows.subject: ST-M O E
rows.operation_detail: Manually classified experts by the coherence of their top-10 decoded vocabulary words after projecting output vectors through the unembedding matrix.
rows.note: The paper describes these as experts that read one concept and write another; it does not say whether they have one main job under the claim's definition.
rows.check: Functional transformers (8%) read one concept and write another. Under the essay's criterion these could count as having one main job, so the row cannot be scored against the version.

rows.subject: ST-M O E
rows.operation_detail: Manually classified experts by the coherence of their top-10 decoded vocabulary words after projecting output vectors through the unembedding matrix.
rows.note: The paper describes these experts as absorbing high-frequency tokens and tokenizer artifacts; it does not classify them under the claim's one-main-job criterion.
rows.check: Garbage collectors (12%) absorb frequent tokens and artifacts. Whether that counts as one job is undefined, so the row is fine as cannot_determine.

rows.subject: ST-M O E
rows.operation_detail: Manually classified experts by the coherence of their top-10 decoded vocabulary words after projecting output vectors through the unembedding matrix.
rows.note: This reported share is substantially unlike the claim's estimate of about 90% of poles with one main job, but the paper's expert classification and the claim's pole explanations are not the same measurement.
rows.check: 'Moderately polysemantic' (65%) is not defined. It may include units the essay would score as having one main job or two related jobs, since only the top-10 output words were inspected. 'Partial' overstates what the row shows.

relationships.condition: 76–84M rank-1 cosine-routed MoE on WikiText-103, experts judged by manual inspection of top-10 unembedding-decoded output words
relationships.reason: Only about 15% of experts are clear single-category specialists (R1), far below about 90%. The remaining categories (R2–R4) are not defined in a way comparable to one main job, so this qualifies rather than refutes V2 under an output-only, small-model measure.
relationships.display_finding: About 15% of experts were clear single-category specialists, far below about 90%. The other categories do not map onto one main job, and the measure uses only output words in a small model.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: 76–84M rank-1 cosine-routed MoE on WikiText-103, experts judged by manual inspection of top-10 unembedding-decoded output words
source_check.reason: About 15% clear specialists is far below 90%, but the measure is stricter, output-only and expert-level. The other classes cannot be mapped to one main job, so the result qualifies V2 and does not refute it.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

labels.reason: About 15% clear specialists is far below 90%, but the measure is stricter, output-only and expert-level. The other classes cannot be mapped to one main job, so the result qualifies V2 and does not refute it.

relation.reason: Reports a share of coherent units in an MoE model, which bears on V2.

tranche.reason: Different method (unembedding decoding of expert outputs, manual labels) on the share of single-job units.

source_check.notes: The 15/8/12/65 split comes from one sentence of manual inspection, with no rater count, rubric or agreement figure; the unit is the rank-1 expert (one Wdown, one SiLU, one Wup, so effectively a single neuron), judged from decoded Wup words, though the 'functional transformer' class implies some input-side reading the text does not describe. The paper also reports 73.5% of experts unclustered by HDBSCAN (Limitations), and calls experts 'monosemantic by construction' despite the 65% moderately polysemantic share.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: The study's 76–84M-parameter ST-M O E model, evaluated on WikiText-103
reader_labels.reason: Only approximately 15% of experts were classified as clear monosemantic specialists, while 65% were classified as moderately polysemantic; these results do not match the proposed similar shares. See R1 and R4.
